clue.text: Walter !

parts.note: the exclamation of surprise doubles as praise for Sir Walter, the Scottish novelist of Waverley and Ivanhoe, as an eminent writer

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott, author of Ivanhoe, was a great writer, so the old cry of astonishment also describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned exclamation of astonishment, and also a fair description of the eminent novelist Sir Walter.

clue.text: Between one and two hundred engaged in singing Rossini

indicators.note: the letters are held within the words singing Rossini, as if engaged there

explanation.surface: Over a hundred performers take part in a Rossini concert.
explanation.definitionFit: A dozen dozen, which is 144, falls between one and two hundred.

clue.text: Moral improvement in the architect's view

explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word between the definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Uplift of the spirit, and the flat drawing of one face of a building made by an architect.

clue.text: Bread for "Vita" office personnel

explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word. Vita is Latin for life, so the workers of Life magazine are its staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverbial name for bread as the basic food, and also the employees of a magazine called Life, vita being Latin for life.

clue.text: In Lucca I'm known as a Limey

indicators.note: the letters of the Italian town and 'I'm' are given a new form, known by another arrangement

explanation.surface: An English visitor in an Italian town is called a Limey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limey' is not the slang for a Briton but means lime-like: lime is an oxide of this element.
explanation.definitionFit: The chemical element whose oxide is quicklime, so it is the limy element.

clue.text: Fast hat ?

parts.note: the highest ratio of a car's gearbox is for speed, and a top hat is headgear worn on top

explanation.definitionFit: The highest gear of a motor car, for driving fast, read also as headwear on the crown.

clue.text: Post of bodyguard

explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link word between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Post is letters delivered; chain armour worn to guard the body is also called by this word.

clue.text: Deck trouble the Navy has

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A sailor complains that the Navy has trouble on deck.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck is to decorate.

clue.text: May swarm's worth for the graminivorous

definitions.text: May swarm's worth for the graminivorous

parts.words: May swarm's worth for the graminivorous
parts.note: an old country rhyme values a swarm of bees in May, and grass-eating animals would value the same quantity of dried grass

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme runs 'A swarm of bees in May is worth a load of hay'; graminivorous means grass-eating.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial value of a May swarm of bees, and a fine meal for grass-eaters such as cattle.

clue.text: Tucker's tucker

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme boy Tommy Tucker sang for his supper, and tucker is slang for food

explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Little Tommy Tucker sings for his supper and is given brown bread and butter; tucker is slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Basic everyday food, which is what the nursery-rhyme boy was given for his supper.

clue.text: A ring as part of a watch

parts.note: a, as a number, is one
a bell is something that rings, a ring of the bell

explanation.surface: Someone describes the ring on a wristwatch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'watch' is a ship's watch, a four-hour duty marked by bells: the first half-hour is struck with a single bell.
explanation.definitionFit: On board ship, time within each four-hour duty period is told by strokes of a bell, one stroke marking its first half-hour.

clue.text: Grape, lo, as trained on a trellis

indicators.note: a vine is trained along supports, so these letters are bent into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A vine is shown being trained up a garden trellis.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed reads 'to'; the printed page has 'lo'. 'trained' rearranges GRAPELO.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden walkway framed by a trellis or arched framework over which climbing plants are grown.

clue.text: The way of those with a leaning to learning?

definitions.text: The way of those with a leaning to learning?

parts.words: The way of those with a leaning to learning?
parts.note: a tilt or leaning is a slant and learning makes one wise, so the manner of the learned-inclined is a sloping one

explanation.definitionFit: The word means obliquely or at an angle, built from a word for a tilt and a suffix meaning in the manner of.

clue.text: Not exactly any small house in Northants

indicators.note: the word any appears not exactly as written but with its letters rearranged

parts.note: ho is the standard abbreviation of house

explanation.surface: A Northamptonshire cottage is said to be not quite like any other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not exactly' rearranges ANY to AYN. Northants is Northamptonshire, an English Midlands county.
explanation.definitionFit: A village in the English county of Northamptonshire, near Banbury.

clue.text: Legal pantie ?

parts.note: a lawyer's case papers share their name with a skimpy piece of underwear

explanation.definitionFit: A barrister's instructions in a case, and in the plural an item of close-fitting underpants.

clue.text: Sweet shy girl with muddy feet

definitions.text: Sweet shy girl with muddy feet

parts.words: Sweet shy girl with muddy feet
parts.note: a shy girl is a shrinking violet, and muddy feet put her in wet marshy ground

explanation.definitionFit: A plant of wet marshy ground with violet-like flowers, pictured as a shy girl standing in mud.

clue.text: Hogarthian Progressive in a damp part of Morocco

indicators.note: the rake's letters sit within the wet land, as the clue says one is in the other

parts.note: damp ground, a marsh or bog
Hogarth's series of paintings is A Rake's Progress, so his progressing figure is the rake's

explanation.surface: A figure from a Hogarth series is placed in a wet corner of North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: William Hogarth painted the series A Rake's Progress; RAKES goes inside MARSH.
explanation.definitionFit: A major city of Morocco, the old imperial capital at the foot of the Atlas mountains.

clue.text: Herb looks well taking a turn on the A I brother, with horsepower

parts.note: eu is the Greek prefix meaning well, as in eulogy

indicators.note: these pieces turn round, reading back to front

parts.note: taken as written
hp is the abbreviation for horsepower

explanation.surface: A herb is said to be healthy while touring the Great North Road with a brother and a powerful car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking a turn' reverses AIBROHP to PHORBIA; 'looks', 'on the' and 'with' are links. The A1 is Britain's Great North Road.
explanation.definitionFit: A spurge, a large genus of plants with milky sap, including poinsettia.

clue.text: Foreigner in a row in the Gilbert and Sullivan partnership ?

definitions.text: Foreigner in a row in the Gilbert and Sullivan partnership ?

parts.words: Foreigner in a row in the Gilbert and Sullivan partnership ?
parts.note: a Venetian oarsman rows his boat, and Gilbert and Sullivan wrote an operetta about two of them

explanation.walkthrough: The 'row' is rowing a boat, not a quarrel; The Gondoliers is a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta set in Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: A Venetian boatman who propels his craft with an oar, the title figures of a Savoy opera.

clue.text: The opposite of prosy ?

parts.note: the reverse of prose is poetry, and something written as poetry is in metre

explanation.definitionFit: Opposite or reversed, and split it reads as written in poetry, the opposite of prose.

clue.text: For no common steed's champ -rabbit it !

parts.note: rare means uncommon
a horse champs at the bit in its mouth

explanation.surface: A horse champs on something unusual, and a rabbit comes into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Welsh rabbit is another name for Welsh rarebit, cheese on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rabbit and Welsh rarebit are the same cheese-on-toast dish.

clue.text: Mad to be wanting to bathe

explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link word between the definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy or silly in slang, and read as dip plus -y, inclined to take a dip.

clue.text: To drive is not exactly simple without Bob

indicators.note: the remaining letters are not exactly as written, being rearranged
the shilling's letter is taken out of the word simple

parts.note: bob is slang for a shilling, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Driving is said to be harder than it looks once Bob is gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes S (a bob, or shilling, was an old British coin) from SIMPLE, leaving IMPLE; 'is not exactly' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: To propel or urge forward is to force onward.

clue.text: Chooses tools.

explanation.definitionFit: Selects, and pointed implements for breaking ground.

clue.text: "Through-glooms and winding mossy ways " (Keats)

parts.note: fill the gap in a line from Keats's Ode to a Nightingale with the word he used for leafy green

explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale has 'Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the Keats line, meaning green with lush vegetation.

clue.text: Nice's rebuilding came later

indicators.note: the letters of the French city are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: The rebuilding of a Riviera town happened afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'came' is a link; the 's of Nice's gives its S to the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as in 'has since moved', meaning subsequently.

clue.text: Fallen match

explanation.definitionFit: The fallen angel Satan bore this name before his fall, and an early friction match was called by it too.

clue.text: Pump-room hair-do and refreshment

parts.note: the Pump Room is the famous Georgian assembly room in the spa town of Bath
a bun is hair coiled at the back of the head

explanation.surface: A spa visitor has a hair appointment and then afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pump Room is in Bath, the English spa city.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet currant roll eaten as a snack with tea, originally from the spa city.

clue.text: Rubbish to get shot of

parts.note: nonsense is talk worth discarding, something to be rid of

explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense or worthless stuff, the sort of thing one wants rid of.

clue.text: Hardly the best route for a Freeman of the City

definitions.text: Hardly the best route for a Freeman of the City

parts.words: Hardly the best route for a Freeman of the City
parts.note: a free man would avoid a road named after shackles, though this one is a street in the City of London

explanation.walkthrough: Fetter Lane is a street in the City of London; a freeman would not want fetters.
explanation.definitionFit: A street in the City of London whose name suggests chains, unsuitable for someone free.
